kcet|Physics|2007|7|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch:
The sound is Doppler-shifted **twice**: once on the way to the wall, and again on the way
back to the moving driver.
**Step 1 — the wall receives the sound.** The wall is a stationary **observer** and the
engine a source moving **towards** it at 50 m s⁻¹:
f₁ = f × v/(v − v_s)
= 1200 × 350/(350 − 50)
= 1200 × 350/300
= **1400 Hz**
**Step 2 — the wall re-emits it.** A reflecting wall acts as a **stationary source** of
the frequency it received, **1400 Hz** ✓
**Step 3 — the driver receives the echo.** Now the driver is an **observer moving
towards** a stationary source at 50 m s⁻¹:
f₂ = f₁ × (v + v_o)/v
= 1400 × (350 + 50)/350
= 1400 × 400/350
= **1600 Hz = 1·6 kHz** ✓
**Why two shifts and not one.** The engine both **emits** and **hears** while moving, so
it gains a shift at each stage ✓ Applying the formula once would give only 1400 Hz, which
is not among the options — the examiner's way of checking that both stages are seen.
**A shortcut for this case.** When the source and observer are the same moving object
reflecting off a stationary wall, the two shifts combine to
f₂ = f(v + v_s)/(v − v_s)
= 1200(400)/(300)
= **1600 Hz** ✓ in one step.
**Which formula goes where.** A **moving source** changes the **wavelength**, so v_s
appears in the **denominator**; a **moving observer** changes the **relative speed** of
the wave, so v_o appears in the **numerator** ✓ Getting them the right way round is the
whole difficulty.
**Reading the distractors.**
**1·2 kHz** ✗ is the original note, as if no shift occurred.
**2·4 kHz** ✗ is double it, which would need a much larger speed ratio.
**0·24 kHz** ✗ is a tenth of that and far below the emitted note — but approaching a wall
can only **raise** the pitch ✓ so any answer below 1·2 kHz is wrong on sight.
**The beat note.** The driver hears the direct note at 1·2 kHz alongside the echo at
1·6 kHz, giving **400 beats per second** — far too fast to count, but the rising pitch of
the echo is exactly what one hears when driving towards a cliff ✓
∴ 1·6 kHz.

kcet|Physics|2007|8|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch.s:
Filling half the tube with water does two things at once — it **halves the air column**
and turns an **open** pipe into a **closed** one — and the two effects exactly cancel.
**Step 1 — the original tube.** Open at both ends, of length L, its fundamental has
wavelength **2L**:
**f = v/(2L)**
**Step 2 — after half-filling.** The air column is now **L/2** long, open at the top but
**closed** at the water surface. A closed pipe's fundamental has wavelength **4 × (air
column)**:
λ' = 4 × (L/2) = **2L**
so
f' = v/(2L) = **f** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** The two frequencies are the **same**: **f′ = f** ✓
**Why the effects cancel.** Halving the length alone would **double** the frequency.
Changing from an open pipe to a closed one alone would **halve** it, since a closed pipe
of a given length sounds an octave below an open pipe of the same length ✓ Doing both at
once leaves the frequency untouched.
**A numerical check.** Take L = 1 m and v = 340 m s⁻¹.
open tube, 1 m: f = 340/(2 × 1) = **170 Hz**
half-filled, air column 0·5 m, closed: f' = 340/(4 × 0·5) = 340/2 = **170 Hz** ✓ equal.
**The two formulas, side by side.**
**open at both ends**, length ℓ: fundamental **v/(2ℓ)** — a full half-wavelength fits
**closed at one end**, length ℓ: fundamental **v/(4ℓ)** — only a quarter-wavelength fits
Here ℓ halves **and** the formula's divisor doubles from 2 to 4, so the product 2ℓ is
unchanged ✓
**Reading the distractors.**
**f′ = 2f** ✗ accounts for the halved length but keeps the pipe **open** — the commonest
error, since it is easy to forget that the water forms a closed end.
**f′ = f/2** ✗ applies the open-to-closed change but forgets that the length also halved.
**f′ = 4f** ✗ combines both errors in the same direction.
The question is built so that exactly one of the two changes, taken alone, gives each
distractor ✓
∴ f′ = f.

Note: the printed key gives the third option, f′ = 2f. That is the frequency if the tube
stayed open at both ends; but the water surface forms a **closed** end, so the
fundamental is v/(4 × L/2) = v/(2L) = f, as the numerical check confirms. The key has been
corrected to the first option.

kcet|Physics|2009|16|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
Immersing part of the tube shortens the air column **and** turns the open pipe into a
closed one — both must be accounted for.
**Step 1 — use the original frequency to fix v/L.** The tube is open at both ends, of
length L:
f = v/(2L) = 390 Hz
so
**v/L = 780**
**Step 2 — find the new air column.** With one quarter immersed, three quarters remains
above the water:
air column = **3L/4**
and the water surface forms a **closed** end ✓
**Step 3 — apply the closed-pipe formula.**
f' = v/(4 × air column)
= v/(4 × 3L/4)
= **v/(3L)**
**Step 4 — substitute.**
f' = 780/3 = **260 Hz** ✓
**Why the frequency falls.** The two changes pull in opposite directions:
shortening the column from L to 3L/4 would **raise** the pitch by a factor 4/3
closing one end **lowers** it by a factor 2
and the net effect is (4/3)/2 = **2/3**, so 390 × 2/3 = **260 Hz** ✓ The closing wins, and
the note drops.
**A direct check.** With v = 340 m s⁻¹, the original tube has
L = v/(2f) = 340/780 = **0·436 m**
The air column is then 3(0·436)/4 = **0·327 m**, and a closed pipe of that length sounds
f' = 340/(4 × 0·327) = **260 Hz** ✓
**Reading the distractors.**
**390 Hz** ✗ assumes nothing changes.
**520 Hz** ✗ = 390 × 4/3 — the shortening accounted for but the pipe wrongly kept
**open**, which is the commonest error here.
**130 Hz** ✗ = 390/3 — an over-correction, as if the column were reduced to a third.
**The general result.** For an open tube of fundamental f with a fraction x immersed, the
new fundamental is
f' = f/[2(1 − x)]
Here x = 1/4 gives f/[2(3/4)] = **2f/3** = 260 Hz ✓ and note that immersing **half**
(x = 1/2) would give exactly f — the companion question, where the two effects cancel.
∴ 260 Hz.

kcet|Physics|2010|8|MTG Karnataka-CET Ch.s:
Express both fundamentals in terms of the common length, use the given beat count to fix
them, then rescale.
**Step 1 — write the two original fundamentals.** For a common length L:
closed pipe: **f_c = v/(4L)**
open pipe: **f_o = v/(2L) = 2f_c**
**Step 2 — use the beat count.** Beats per second equal the difference in frequency:
f_o − f_c = 2f_c − f_c = **f_c** = 2
so
**f_c = 2 Hz** and **f_o = 4 Hz**
(and hence v/L = 8, in whatever units the numbers imply — only the **ratios** matter.)
**Step 3 — halve the open pipe.** Its new length is L/2:
f_o′ = v/(2 × L/2) = v/L = **8 Hz**
— twice its old value, since halving the length doubles the frequency ✓
**Step 4 — double the closed pipe.** Its new length is 2L:
f_c′ = v/(4 × 2L) = v/(8L) = **1 Hz**
— half its old value ✓
**Step 5 — find the new beats.**
|f_o′ − f_c′| = |8 − 1| = **7 beats per second** ✓
**A table of the four frequencies.**
open, length L: **4** → halved to L/2: **8**
closed, length L: **2** → doubled to 2L: **1**
beats before: 4 − 2 = **2** ✓ matching the question
beats after: 8 − 1 = **7** ✓
**Why the closed pipe sounds an octave lower.** A closed pipe fits only a **quarter**
wavelength in its length, an open pipe a **half** ✓ so for the same length the closed pipe
has twice the wavelength and half the frequency — which is what makes f_o = 2f_c and lets
the single beat figure pin both down.
**Reading the distractors.**
**8** ✗ is the new **open-pipe frequency** alone, not the difference — the commonest slip,
since 8 is so prominent in the working.
**6** ✗ would follow from 8 − 2, leaving the closed pipe unchanged.
**2** ✗ is the original beat count, as if the changes cancelled.
**The check that settles it.** The two pipes move **apart** in frequency — one doubles,
the other halves — so the beat rate must **increase** from 2 ✓ and the exact figure is
8 − 1 = 7.
∴ 7.

Note: the printed key gives the third option, 8. The new frequencies are 8 Hz and 1 Hz,
whose difference is 7; the value 8 is the open pipe's frequency rather than the beat rate.
The key has been corrected to the fourth option.

kcet|Physics|2011|22|MTG Karnataka-CET C:
Write the fundamental in terms of everything that changes, then track each factor.
**Step 1 — state the formula.** For a stretched wire of length L, tension T and linear
density μ:
f = (1/2L)√(T/μ)
and with μ = ρπr² for a wire of radius r:
f = (1/2L)√(T/(ρπr²)) = **(1/(2L r))√(T/(ρπ))**
so, for the same material,
**f ∝ √T/(L r)**
**Step 2 — apply each change.**
length **doubled**: L → 2L, so f is divided by **2**
radius **halved**: r → r/2, so f is multiplied by **2**
tension **one-ninth**: T → T/9, so √T is divided by **3**
**Step 3 — combine.**
f′/f = (1/2) × 2 × (1/3) = **1/3**
The length and radius changes **cancel exactly**, leaving only the tension ✓
**Step 4 — compute.**
f′ = 600/3 = **200 Hz** ✓
**Why the length and radius cancel.** Both appear to the **first** power in the
denominator, so doubling one and halving the other leaves the product Lr unchanged ✓ The
wire is twice as long but half as thick, and those effects are exactly opposed.
**Why the tension contributes only a third.** It enters under a **square root**, so
dividing T by 9 divides f by √9 = **3** — not by 9 ✓ That square root is the single most
common place to go wrong here.
**A check with numbers.** Take f = 600 Hz with L = 1 m, r = 1 mm and some T. Then
L r = 1 × 10⁻³ before, and (2)(0·5 × 10⁻³) = **10⁻³** after ✓ unchanged, so
f′ = 600 × √(1/9) = 600/3 = **200 Hz** ✓
**Reading the distractors.**
**600 Hz** ✗ would mean all three changes cancelled — two do, but the tension does not.
**300 Hz** ✗ = 600/2, as if the tension change gave a factor of 1/2 (or as if only the
length changed).
**400 Hz** ✗ = 600 × 2/3, which no combination of these factors produces.
**The general rule.** f ∝ √T · L⁻¹ · r⁻¹, so scaling T by t, L by ℓ and r by ρ scales the
frequency by **√t/(ℓρ)** ✓ Here √(1/9)/(2 × 1/2) = (1/3)/1 = 1/3.
∴ 200 Hz.
